title: Reverse a Singly Linked List
statement:
A singly linked list only ever points forward: each `Node` knows its own
`next`, and nothing knows its previous node unless something keeps track.
Reversing the list means every node's `next` has to end up pointing the
other way -- and the moment you overwrite a node's `next`, its old
downstream neighbour is gone forever unless you saved a pointer to it
first.

## The type

```
struct Node
{
    int value;
    Node* next;
};
```

## Your function

```
Node* ReverseList(Node* head);
```

Reverse the list starting at `head` **iteratively, in place, using O(1)
extra space** -- no recursion, no new nodes, no container copying the
values out and back in. Return a pointer to the new head (the old tail).
`head` may be `nullptr`, meaning an empty list.

## Watch out

- **Save `current->next` before you overwrite it.** The instant
  `current->next` is pointed backwards, the only remaining way to reach
  the rest of the original list -- everything that used to come after
  `current` -- is a pointer you saved *before* that assignment ran. Do it
  after, and the rest of the list is unreachable: not corrupted, not
  crashed, just permanently lost, which is the kind of bug that only shows
  up on a list with more than two or three nodes.
- **Three pointers, not two, are enough: `prev`, `current`, and a
  temporary for `current`'s original `next`.** `prev` starts at `nullptr`
  (there is nothing before the first node); by the time the loop ends,
  `current` is `nullptr` and `prev` is sitting on the last node visited --
  the new head -- which is what the function returns, not `current`.
- **`head == nullptr` needs no special case.** The loop condition is
  simply "while there is a current node", which is false immediately for
  an empty list, and the function correctly returns `prev`, still
  `nullptr`, without ever having entered the loop body.

tests.name: an empty list reverses to itself
several nodes reverse completely, not just the first link
tests.description: A solution that forgets to save next before overwriting it typically loses everything after the first one or two nodes -- check the whole sequence, not just the front.

tests.name: negative and repeated values reverse like any others
